label: Constant front-to-back growth ratio makes the rhinoceros horn a logarithmic spiral
notation: v_{ant}/v_{post} = \rho = \text{const},\ w = \beta s \Rightarrow s = s_0 e^{\theta\cot\alpha},\ \cot\alpha = \beta/(\rho - 1)
assumptions: Anterior side grows at a constant multiple rho > 1 of the posterior growth rate; bending through d(theta) lengthens the outer side over the inner by the horn's width (ds_out - ds_in = w d(theta)); width proportional to length (w = beta s, constant taper); posterior length differentiable in the turning angle theta.
scope_note: Proves the horn's length grows exponentially in its turning angle, s = s0 e^{theta cot alpha}, which is the intrinsic (Whewell) equation of a logarithmic spiral of constant angle alpha; the claims.json polar form r = a e^{theta cot alpha} is equivalent but was restated in the form actually proved. The plane (untwisted) character follows from the median position by symmetry and is not formalized here (see ch13-06). Whether real horns have constant growth ratio and taper is empirical.

label: Constant unequal growth on opposite sides gives a continuous, self-similar horn spiral
assumptions: Same growth model as ch13-01: growth rates on two opposite sides in constant ratio rho > 1 throughout growth, bending equal to width per unit turning, width proportional to length.
scope_note: Proves that every further turning through phi multiplies the horn by the same factor at any stage of growth (the spiral is continuous and self-similar), and that the spiral constant cot alpha decreases as the growth inequality rho grows, so nearly equal growth gives a nearly straight horn. The polar notation of claims.json was restated as the self-similarity actually proved. That this holds in the great majority of horns is empirical.

label: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
reason: Empirical generalization from Thompson's measurements of spiral angles in particular species; there is no mathematical inference to prove, only measured values to check against horn data.

label: Fastest and slowest horn growth share a plane with the axis iff diametrically opposite
assumptions: The directions of maximal and minimal growth are distinct unit directions (angles phi1, phi2) around the circular basal growth zone; a plane spiral requires both to lie in a single plane through the horn's axis.
scope_note: Proves the geometric core: two distinct points of the basal annulus lie in one plane with the axis exactly when they are diametrically opposite. The notation was restated in the form proved. That non-coplanar extremes produce a helical component, and that real horns usually lack such a plane of symmetry, are Thompson's physical assertions and left to a three-dimensional growth model and data.

label: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal accretion are log spirals, conspicuous when long
assumptions: Same accretionary growth model as the horn (ch13-01): permanent increments, constant ratio rho > 1 of growth on opposite sides, width proportional to length, beta > 0, initial length positive.
scope_note: Proves the structure is a logarithmic spiral whose turning angle grows only as the logarithm of its length (theta = tan alpha log(s/s0)), so the spiral becomes visible only when the structure is long. The notation was restated as proved. Whether nails, claws, beaks and teeth meet the model's assumptions is empirical.

label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair entails every lower pair down to (1, 1)
notation: F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1} (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots); pair (F_n, F_{n+1}) present \Rightarrow all lower pairs present
assumptions: Tait's construction: in a system with one genetic spiral, a parastichy pair (m, n) implies the pair (n, m - n) in the same system (the leaf S reached by n and m - n steps).
scope_note: Proves that Tait's reduction step maps each consecutive Fibonacci pair to the next lower one and that iterating it from (F_{k+2}, F_{k+1}) passes through every lower pair and ends at (1, 1). The geometric step itself (existence of the leaf S on the unwrapped cylinder) is taken as Thompson's construction, not derived from a lattice model.

label: Between two and three leaves per turn (t = 2) gives the Fibonacci parastichy series
notation: G_0 = 1,\ G_1 = t,\ G_{n+2} = G_n + G_{n+1};\ t = 2 \Rightarrow G_n = F_{n+2} (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots);\ t = 3 \Rightarrow 1, 3, 4, 7, \dots
assumptions: The parastichy series of a system is generated upward from its lowest pair (1, t) by the inverse of Tait's step, (m, n) -> (m + n, m).
scope_note: Proves that t = 2 generates exactly the Fibonacci numbers and that t = 3 generates a different series (it contains 4, which is not a Fibonacci number). The notation was restated as the recurrence proved. That t = 2 holds in the great majority of fir-cones and other plants is empirical.

label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
notation: conspicuous parastichies set by the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area, not by the divergence angle
reason: Conspicuousness is a perceptual property with no mathematical definition, and Thompson states he did not investigate the mathematics; any Lean statement would have to invent the criterion of what the eye catches.

label: Phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, … converge to the golden mean (√5 − 1)/2
assumptions: Phyllotactic fractions are ratios F_n / F_{n+1} of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
scope_note: Proves the mathematical fact Thompson cites: F_n / F_{n+1} tends to (√5 − 1)/2. His conclusion that this is a coincidence without biological significance is a conceptual judgement that mathematics cannot establish.

label: Egg equation p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P: external pressure flattens the egg
notation: p_n + T/r + T'/r' = P; with equal tensions p_n + T(1/r + 1/r') = P
assumptions: Membrane equilibrium p_n + T(1/r + 1/r') = P holds at each point (taken as the postulate); tension T > 0 and internal pressure P the same over the egg.
scope_note: Takes the Laplace membrane equation as the stated law and proves its consequences: it reduces from unequal to equal tensions, a point under greater external pressure has smaller total curvature, and uniform external pressure forces constant total curvature. The equation itself is not derived from membrane mechanics; oviduct pressures and egg curvatures are empirical.

label: Vessel wall thickness ∝ radius at constant pressure, relatively thinner as pressure falls
notation: P = T/R,\ T = \sigma t \Rightarrow t = (P/\sigma) R;\ P_2 < P_1 \Rightarrow t_2/R_2 < t_1/R_1
assumptions: Cylindrical vessel, external support neglected (P = T/R); tension proportional to wall thickness with the same stress sigma > 0 in all vessels; R > 0.
scope_note: Proves wall thickness is proportional to radius at constant pressure and that a vessel at lower pressure has a smaller thickness-to-radius ratio. The notation was extended to state both results. That pressure actually falls from large arteries to capillaries, and by how much, is empirical.

label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the chamber's mean curvature
notation: t(1/r + 1/r') = C within each cavity of the heart
assumptions: Uniform pressure P within a cavity; Laplace's law P = T(1/r + 1/r') at each point; tension proportional to wall thickness, T = sigma t with the same sigma > 0 over the wall; positive curvature.
scope_note: Proves t(1/r + 1/r') = P/sigma, the same constant C at every point of a cavity, and that the more curved region is thinner. That real myocardium carries equal stress per unit thickness (so that the apex is the thinnest) is empirical.

label: Equally dilated ventricles have wall-thickness ratio equal to their pressure ratio
notation: t_L/t_R = P_L/P_R \text{ at equal curvature};\ P_L/P_R \approx 6\text{--}7 \text{ (measured)}
assumptions: Both ventricles dilated to the same curvature (equal and symmetric dilation); same tension per unit thickness sigma > 0; heart-wall law of ch15-11; P_R > 0.
scope_note: Proves that at equal curvature the thickness ratio equals the dilating-pressure ratio. The value 6–7 is Thompson's measurement and is left to data; the notation was restated to separate the proved relation from the measured value.

label: Optimal arterial branching angle has cos x = L/L′, trunk-to-branch energy-loss ratio
notation: \cos x = L/L', L and L' the energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch
assumptions: Hess's model: blood travels along a straight trunk at loss L per unit length, then along a straight branch to a target at lateral distance h ≠ 0 at loss L' > 0 per unit length; total loss E(u) = L(D - u) + L' sqrt(u^2 + h^2), with u the remaining axial distance and cos x = u / sqrt(u^2 + h^2).
scope_note: Proves the energy loss is stationary in the branching point exactly when cos x = L/L', Thompson's (Hess's) equal-neighbouring-routes argument; global minimality is not proved separately. Real energy losses per unit length and branch angles are empirical.
